messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Kwame was a 20-year-old African man who had come to the clinic after months of feeling as though something in him had broken and not returned. A single, unmarried doctor, he had prided himself on being calm under pressure, the kind of person patients and coworkers could look to in an emergency. That certainty began to unravel during a combat deployment when his unit came under fire and the air around him changed all at once: gunshots, people shouting, and then the terrifying, unnatural silence that followed when the firing stopped and he could hear his own breathing. He later described that breathing as sharp and labored, as if his chest had forgotten how to work. In the aftermath, those moments returned to him not as a full story but in disconnected pieces that would flash up and then slip away. He found himself pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it, and there were stretches he simply could not reconstruct no matter how hard he tried.

Since coming home, Kwame had become convinced that the attack had done more than frighten him. It had destroyed the assumptions he had lived by. He spoke with a quiet bitterness about no longer knowing himself, as if the man who had once wanted to heal people and trust his own judgment had been replaced by someone unfamiliar and permanently altered. What unsettled him most was that ordinary life no longer felt ordinary: sudden silence in a corridor, the pause after a conversation stops, or the sensation of being short of breath during a rushed hospital shift could send him back into the feeling that danger was near. Violence on a television screen or even a heated argument nearby sharpened that sense immediately. Each of these moments seemed to confirm his belief that the world did not work the way he had been taught, and that he had to stay on guard all the time because safety could vanish without warning.

That way of thinking made the memories harder to face. When images or fragments rose up, he would clamp down on them before they became too clear, afraid that if he let the scene come into focus he would be overwhelmed by what it meant about him and about the world. He noticed that the more he tried not to remember, the more the event returned in broken pieces: a flash of dust, the pressure in his chest, the instant of silence after the violence, and then blankness. Those gaps only deepened his sense that something essential was missing, and that he was perhaps missing part of himself with it. In that state, he became even more alert to anything that could hint at threat. He watched faces, listened for changes in tone, and especially reacted to breathlessness in his own body, interpreting it as a sign that danger was close or that he was losing control again.

At work, these moments had begun to intrude into the practical rhythm of being a doctor. During long shifts, when a patient room suddenly went quiet or when he felt himself needing to catch his breath, the old fear returned with enough force that he would excuse himself, step into the hallway, and stand listening for sounds that reassured him. He avoided unnecessary exposure to violence in news reports and shrank away from conversations about conflict, but he could not avoid the hospital environment, where emergencies and silence could appear without warning. Over weeks, that constant watchfulness and the effort to keep the memory at bay left him more exhausted and less certain of his place among colleagues. He said he had started to feel as if he was acting the part of a doctor rather than being one, because the confidence he used to trust no longer felt like his own.

By the time he sought help, Kwame was frightened less by the original event than by the way it kept organizing his present. He was afraid he would keep losing pieces of the memory, and with them whatever was left of his identity, but he was also afraid that if he remembered too much he would be unable to bear what it said about the world. He came in hoping to understand why silence and breathlessness had become so powerful, and whether he could ever feel like himself again without always having to stand guard.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph clearly shows triggers/reminders causing negative appraisals; the cues are described as increasing threat and alertness, but not as leading to negative beliefs or appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph states that negative appraisals drive the traumatic memory to return or intensify.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph shows negative appraisals causing triggers or reminders to arise.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph explicitly shows the traumatic memory leading to negative appraisals; the vignette links memory fragments to fear and threat, but not to beliefs about self or world.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph explicitly shows the traumatic memory causing triggers/reminders; the cues are presented as eliciting threat, but not as being produced by the memory.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Since coming home, Kwame had become convinced that the attack had done more than frighten him. It had destroyed the assumptions he had lived by.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Once he settled on that conclusion, ordinary cues began to feel loaded with meaning: a silence in a corridor or a sudden pause in conversation no longer seemed neutral, but like proof that danger could return without warning. Each reminder fed the same belief that the world was unsafe and that he could not trust his own sense of when things were about to go wrong.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
That way of thinking made the memories harder to face. When images or fragments rose up, he would clamp down on them before they became too clear, afraid that if he let the scene come into focus he would be overwhelmed by what it meant about him and about the world.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The more he tried to keep the belief at bay, the more the memory seemed to push back into view, as if the mind kept returning him to the moment in order to prove how deeply it had changed him. When the scene came back, it carried the same conviction with it: that something in him had been permanently altered by what happened.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Since coming home, Kwame had become convinced that the attack had done more than frighten him. It had destroyed the assumptions he had lived by.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Because he had come to see himself as permanently changed and on guard, almost anything could turn into a reminder — a raised voice in the hospital corridor, the wrong kind of silence after a room emptied, or the feel of his own breathing turning shallow on a rushed shift. Those moments did not just startle him; they seemed to confirm his belief that he was now the kind of man who had to scan for threat everywhere.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He found himself pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it, and there were stretches he simply could not reconstruct no matter how hard he tried.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time the memory broke through in fragments, it brought a harsh conclusion with it: that he had not been strong enough, and that this must mean something was wrong with him now. The image of the attack made those beliefs feel less like fears than facts.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The more he tried not to remember, the more the event returned in broken pieces: a flash of dust, the pressure in his chest, the instant of silence after the violence, and then blankness.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Those fragments were enough to make him begin noticing echoes of the event in the present, as if the memory itself had taught him where to look for danger. A sudden hush in a patient room or the sound of his own breath catching could pull his attention there at once, and he would move through the rest of the shift as though those cues were warnings he could not afford to ignore.
<<<END>>>
